title: Chanting in Zen
hookLine: the Heart Sutra, the four vows, the names of the ancestors

cards: Zen has a reputation for silence, so the morning service can come as a surprise. Before breakfast, the whole hall stands or kneels and chants, loudly, in one low, steady pitch.
A hollow wooden drum, carved in the shape of a fish, keeps the beat: tok, tok, tok. Nobody is performing. Nobody is singing harmony.
Voices that don't match blend into one sound that seems to fill the floorboards. Then it stops, and the silence afterward feels different.

teach.b: First, the Heart Sutra. You met it earlier on this path: the short text where Avalokiteshvara sees that all five heaps are empty, and tells Shariputra that form is emptiness and emptiness is form.

Zen halls chant it often, in Japanese, Chinese, Korean, Vietnamese or English, depending on the community. Chanting it isn't studying it. The aim is to let the text pass through the body until it's breath, not argument.

Second, the four vows: the bodhisattva vows, said together, often at the end of a service. In plain paraphrase: beings are without number, I vow to free them. Delusions never run out, I vow to end them.
The gates of the teaching are without limit, I vow to enter them. The Buddha's way is beyond reach, I vow to embody it. Each vow names something impossible, and promises it anyway.
Third, the ancestors. Some services chant the lineage: the Buddha, then teacher after teacher, down to the founders of that community's line.
A family tree said aloud, a reminder that this practice came hand to hand, through people.
Chanting uses breath, belly and throat. It's hard to chant at full voice and think about lunch. And chanting together makes the hall one body, the way kinhin made it one line.
Zen silence and Zen chanting aren't opposites. Both are ways of being entirely here.

how: Zen communities hold chanting services, often morning and evening, where the Heart Sutra, the four bodhisattva vows, dedications and sometimes the names of the lineage ancestors are chanted together in a steady tone, often kept in time by a wooden drum.

o: a solo song performed for visitors at a Zen temple
Zen practice of chanting sutras and vows in one low voice
silent reading of the sutras alone before sitting

s: Zen is entirely silent, with no chanting
Zen halls chant: the Heart Sutra, the four vows, the names of the ancestors.
each of the four vows names something that can't be finished
beings without number, delusions that never run out: promised anyway.
Zen chanting is sung in harmony, like a choir
it's one low, steady pitch, many voices blended into one sound.

games.q: you're chanting the four vows: beings are without number, I vow to free them. a voice in you says that's impossible. what does the vow do with that?
o: keeps the vow anyway, knowing it can't be finished.
changes it to a smaller number.
games.why: the vows name the impossible on purpose. they're said anyway, as a direction to walk in, not a task to complete.

practice: Sit up and take a full breath into the belly.

If you practice, say the four vows in your community's wording; if not, say today's plain paraphrase slowly, in one low, steady tone, from beings are without number through all four, without worrying about perfect words.
Then sit in the quiet that follows.
